claims.text: The reported HfNbTiVAl10 alloy has a hierarchical heterostructure comprising a primary matrix and nano-to-microscale secondary phases or interfacial regions observable by TEM or SEM.

An ML-assisted multiscale simulation explicitly informed by hierarchical-microstructure descriptors will predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior more accurately and efficiently than conventional simulations.
The proposed framework couples ab initio and mesoscale models to an ML surrogate model.
Phase distributions, interfacial bonding, and grain-size variation can be quantified from microscopy and supplied as model inputs.
The proposed model will predict tensile stress–strain behavior and fracture initiation and propagation.
Nanophase dispersions, interfacial bonding characteristics, and phase-distribution statistics mediate local stress concentrations and strain gradients.
Local stress concentrations and strain gradients govern the alloy’s elastic, yielding, and fracture behavior.
Representing microstructural heterogeneity allows the model to capture locally heterogeneous stress and strain fields.
Capturing heterogeneous stress and strain fields improves prediction of stiffness, plastic-yield onset, and fracture-crack paths.
Conventional homogenized simulations do not resolve the relevant microstructural interfaces and defects.
The proposed model will improve predictive accuracy by roughly 20–30% relative to conventional finite-element or atomistic simulations that omit hierarchical heterogeneity.
The proposed model will reduce computational time by approximately a factor of ten.
The approach is applicable when the hierarchical heterostructure is well characterized and remains stable during room-temperature tensile and fracture testing.
Inadequately resolved microstructural features or processing-induced microstructural variation may cause the approach to fail.
Unexpected phases or interfacial phenomena at strain rates or temperatures outside the training domain may cause the approach to fail.
The quantitative accuracy and efficiency gains depend on the quality and representativeness of the training data.
Differences in microstructural characterization may introduce variability into model performance.
